title: The Stations of the Cross
hookLine: fourteen stops from condemnation to the tomb

cards: Fourteen small pictures or carvings hang along the side walls of many Catholic churches, evenly spaced, each with a little cross above it and a Roman numeral underneath. Most weeks nobody pays them much attention.
But on Friday evenings in Lent, the lights dim and a small group gathers at the first one. They stand. They kneel.
They move to the next. Slowly they walk the walls of the church, all the way around, until they end at the tomb.

teach.b: The Stations of the Cross, also called the Way of the Cross, are fourteen stops on Jesus's last journey: from Pilate condemning him, through carrying the cross and the crucifixion, to his body laid in the tomb.

Station comes from the Latin statio, a standing place, a place where you stop. It started in Jerusalem, where for centuries pilgrims walked the road Christians believed Jesus walked, praying where things happened.
That road is called the Via Dolorosa, the way of sorrow.
Few Christians could travel to Jerusalem, so over the Middle Ages, especially through the Franciscans, who looked after the holy places, the walk was brought home.
Churches set up stopping points so anyone could make the pilgrimage in their own parish. The number fourteen was settled in the eighteenth century.
Honestly, some stations come straight from the Gospels, like Simon of Cyrene helping to carry the cross, and Jesus speaking to the women of Jerusalem.
In the Douay-Rheims he says: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not over me; but weep for yourselves, and for your children."
Others come from tradition: Jesus falling three times, meeting his mother on the way, and Veronica wiping his face. The Gospels don't describe those.
In 1991, Pope John Paul the Second led a version with stations drawn only from Scripture, and both forms are prayed today.
At each station, people often say, we adore you, O Christ, and we praise you, because by your holy cross you have redeemed the world. Then a reading, a reflection, a prayer, and on to the next.
The aim is not to watch, but to walk with him.

how: Catholics pray the Stations of the Cross especially on Fridays in Lent, walking or turning from station to station around the church, with a reading, a reflection and a prayer at each.

games.q: you're Jesus, carrying the cross. women of Jerusalem are weeping for you along the road. what do you say?
o: thank them and walk on in silence.
weep not over me; but weep for yourselves, and for your children.
games.why: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not over me; but weep for yourselves, and for your children." even on the way to die, he turns toward them.

practice: Take a few slow steps across the room, or walk in your imagination, and stop three times.

First, Jesus takes up the cross: think of something heavy you're carrying; then Simon helps him: think of someone who helped you carry something; then he meets the women of Jerusalem: think of someone who is grieving.
If you pray, pray at each stop.

wordCard.voice: Stations. From the Latin for a place to stop. Fourteen stops on Jesus's road from condemnation to the tomb, walked around the walls of a church. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a standing place, a post, a stop. It gave us station.

carryVoice: Your line: walk it with him. Tomorrow, the three holiest days begin. One hundred fifty days now.
